Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I have failed in my most important role in life
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, dogs as a trigger is possible but, in the absence of any related memory content, threat theme, or appraisal linking animals to the event, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the profile and is hard to integrate clinically with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal that something about the patient made the event happen is difficult to reconcile with terrorism trauma, which is typically externally caused and indiscriminate. Self-blame can occur, but this specific intrinsic-causation item is not well supported by the rest of the profile and is clinically hard to explain here.

vignette:
Elena Morales, a 78-year-old widow who still worked part-time as a call center agent, traced the beginning of her current life to the afternoon of a bombing at a busy downtown transit plaza where she had been meeting her adult daughter. She remembered the ordinary details before it happened with painful clarity—the heat rising off the pavement, the sound of buses pulling in, her daughter waving from near the benches—and then the scene broke apart. There was a blast, people screaming, bodies dropping, and a force that snapped her head hard enough to leave lasting neck pain. Her daughter was killed there. When Elena tried to describe that day now, she would stop, press her hand to her throat, and say she knew what happened but could not find the words. Whole sections remained missing no matter how hard she searched, and what survived often came back not as a story but as fragments of sound, pressure, and the feeling of her neck locking.

In the months after the attack, the things that reached her most quickly were reminders of loss. At work, when callers spoke about relatives they had lost, even in situations unrelated to violence, Elena felt abruptly pulled back into the plaza. If her neck began to ache during a shift, that pain itself seemed to transport her to the instant of the blast. Any direct conversation about the attack had the same effect. These moments did not bring a clear narrative; instead they brought the unspeakable parts of the experience closer, leaving her with bodily terror, blank spaces, and the humiliating sense that the worst thing that had ever happened to her could not be properly said. Because those reminders so reliably undid her, she began organizing her life around staying away from them.

She refused to go near the transit plaza, even when a shorter route to work would have taken her past it. As the anniversary approached each year, she became vigilant about dates, turning down family invitations and keeping the television off so she would not encounter memorial coverage. She also pulled back from emotional closeness. Friends from church and her surviving family wanted to sit with her and remember her daughter, but Elena would shorten visits or keep the conversation practical, convinced that if she let anyone near her grief, words about the event or about losing loved ones would open something she could not control. That narrowing of her life came to shape her memory of the bombing as much as protect her from it: the less she approached the place, the dates, or other people’s questions, the more the event stayed in disconnected flashes that would not settle into language.

What frightened Elena most was what these experiences seemed to say about her. When reminders of the bombing brought back that wordless terror and those gaps, she had come to believe the attack had broken something essential in her. Not being able to tell the story felt to her like proof of helplessness: bad things happened, and she could do nothing to stop them, then or now. She spoke often of having failed in her most important role in life, meaning that she had not protected her daughter that day. The missing pieces did not soften this belief; they made it harsher, because she filled the silence with certainty that she had failed in some decisive moment she could no longer access. From there it was a short step to saying she had no future, that at her age she was only waiting out what remained.

Her avoidance deepened those conclusions over time. Staying away from the plaza, the anniversaries, and intimate conversations gave her temporary relief, but it also left her increasingly alone with the same bodily fragments and the same unanswered questions. At the call center she had started asking supervisors to reassign calls when customers began talking about bereavement, and she dreaded the neck pain that could flare in her chair because she knew it could unravel the rest of her shift. She no longer trusted herself to comfort others, which only reinforced her sense that she had failed as a mother and now as a person. The more she withdrew from closeness, the more convinced she became that there was nothing left ahead of her except endurance.

By the time Elena sought treatment, the approach of another anniversary had made the pattern impossible to ignore. A caller had recently mentioned losing a son, and Elena froze, rubbing her neck while the old panic and blankness washed over her. She went home and would not answer her granddaughter’s calls for two days. What finally brought her in was not only the distress itself but the fear that she was disappearing from the people she had left. She said, quietly, that she did not know how to live with a memory she could not put into words, and that she wanted help before her last years became nothing but avoiding places, dates, and the people she loved.
